title: Interactive and Experiential Art
answer: Audience-reactive installations, generative AR and VR, dialogue engines, data sculptures and audio-visual systems.

children.name: Audience-Reactive Installations
children.blurb: Audience-reactive installations are artworks that sense the people in front of them and change what they show, play or do in response.

children.name: Generative AR and VR Environments
children.blurb: Generative AR and VR environments cover systems that build or alter three dimensional scenes, avatars and spatial effects in real time, whether the viewer sees them through a headset, a phone camera or a projection.

children.name: Dialogue Engines and Virtual Docents
children.blurb: Dialogue engines and virtual docents are conversational systems built to guide visitors through exhibitions, museums, galleries and public art installations.

children.name: Data Sculpture
children.blurb: Data Sculpture is the practice of turning a dataset into a physical or spatial object that a viewer can walk around, touch, or hear.

children.name: Audio-Visual Systems
children.blurb: Audio-visual systems in interactive and experiential art are installations and performances where sound and moving image are generated, processed or synchronised together, often in response to the presence or actions of an audience.

sections.body: Interactive and experiential art uses artificial intelligence to make works that change with the people in front of them. Cameras, microphones, motion sensors and pressure mats feed live signals into models that classify gestures, track bodies, recognise speech or generate images, and the output is projected, sounded or moved in the room. In practice this means an installation can tell a raised hand from a walking visitor, a virtual docent can answer a spoken question about the objects nearby, and a data sculpture can shift its shape as new numbers arrive. The AI is usually one component inside a larger authored system, doing perception, generation or matching rather than making the aesthetic decisions. Artists work with these tools the way earlier generations worked with video or sensors, treating the model as a material with its own quirks.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The perception side is comparatively settled. Pose estimation, gesture recognition and speech transcription are reliable enough for gallery conditions, and generative image and audio models produce usable material on demand. What remains hard is meaning over time. Systems struggle to hold a coherent relationship with a returning visitor, to remember what happened in an earlier encounter, or to respond in ways that feel authored rather than generic. Latency, lighting, crowd noise and the sheer variety of human behaviour still break installations, and most runs need a technician nearby. Dialogue engines can answer questions but often drift, and generative environments can look impressive while offering little to do. The honest limit is that the interesting part, sustained and legible interaction, is the part least solved.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here divide the field by the kind of encounter and the kind of output. Audience-Reactive Installations covers the broad case of work that senses bodies and responds in the room, and it is the natural starting point for how sensing and feedback are wired together. Generative AR and VR Environments takes that responsiveness into headsets and phone screens, where the space itself is produced by the model. Dialogue Engines and Virtual Docents deals with language, the systems that talk with visitors and guide them through collections or narratives. Data Sculpture turns datasets into physical or projected form, so the AI is often doing translation rather than conversation. Audio-Visual Systems gathers work where sound and image are generated and shaped together, often in response to the same live signals the other pages describe.
